title: Anatomy of a Network Request — URL to Response
summary: Trace one HTTP request end-to-end — DNS, routing, TCP, TLS, and HTTP — tying every other topic in this area into a single mental model of what happens when you hit enter.

slides.markdown:
Typing a URL and hitting enter triggers six distinct phases, each owned by a different layer/protocol: **DNS** resolves the name, **routing** gets packets there, **TCP** opens a reliable connection, **TLS** encrypts it, **HTTP** carries the actual request/response, and the browser **renders** the result.

![Six phases from URL to rendered page: DNS, routing, TCP, TLS, HTTP, render](assets/request-lifecycle-phases.svg)

Each phase is its own deep topic elsewhere in this area — this topic's job is to show how they chain together end-to-end.

assets.alt: Six phases from URL to rendered page: DNS, routing, TCP, TLS, HTTP, render

slides.markdown:
Before anything else, the hostname has to become an IP address. The browser asks a **recursive resolver**, which — if nothing is cached — walks root to TLD to authoritative server:

![DNS resolution: recursive resolver walking root, TLD, and authoritative servers](assets/dns-lookup-mini.svg)

Full mechanics, record types, and caching live in [DNS: Domain Name Resolution](dns-resolution).

assets.alt: DNS resolution: recursive resolver walking root, TLD, and authoritative servers

slides.markdown:
With the destination IP known, every packet still has to travel hop-by-hop — your router, your ISP, backbone links, and the destination's network, each making its own independent forwarding decision:

![The packet's hop-by-hop path through ISP, backbone, and peer AS to the server](assets/route-hops-mini.svg)

How each hop decides is covered in [Routing Fundamentals & Routing Tables](routing-fundamentals).

assets.alt: The packet's hop-by-hop path through ISP, backbone, and peer AS to the server

slides.markdown:
Once a packet can reach the server, the client and server still need a **reliable connection** before any HTTP bytes move — that's the TCP three-way handshake:

![TCP three-way handshake followed by the TLS handshake before HTTP data flows](assets/tcp-tls-handshake-mini.svg)

Detail on sequence numbers, states, and teardown is in [TCP Connection Setup & Teardown](tcp-connection-management).

assets.alt: TCP three-way handshake followed by the TLS handshake before HTTP data flows

slides.markdown:
For `https://` (nearly everything today), a second handshake layers encryption on top of the open TCP connection — exchanging keys and verifying the server's certificate first:

![The TLS handshake exchanging ClientHello, ServerHello, and certificate before an encrypted channel is ready](assets/tcp-tls-handshake-mini.svg)

Detail in [The TLS Handshake](tls-handshake-deep-dive).

assets.alt: The TLS handshake exchanging ClientHello, ServerHello, and certificate before an encrypted channel is ready

slides.markdown:
Only now — after DNS, routing, TCP, and TLS are all done — does the browser send the actual **HTTP request** (method, path, headers) over the encrypted channel, and the server returns a **response** (status, headers, body).

This is the one phase most people picture when they think "a web request," but it's often the smallest slice of total time on a cold connection. Full request/response anatomy is in [HTTP Fundamentals](http-fundamentals).

The full chain rarely runs in full. A **CDN edge** node close to the user can serve a cached response without ever reaching the origin server, skipping most of routing's long haul. A **browser cache** can skip the network entirely for a resource it already has fresh. These short-circuits are why real-world page loads are far faster than the naive six-phase chain suggests — see [CDN & Edge Caching](cdn-edge-caching) for how caches decide what's servable locally.

TCP and TLS handshakes aren't free — each is at least one extra round-trip before any real data moves. **Keep-alive** connections let the browser reuse an already-open, already-encrypted connection for subsequent requests to the same host, skipping phases 3 and 4 entirely.

This is why loading a second page on the same site feels snappier than the first: most of the expensive setup only happens once per connection, not once per request.

| | Cold connection (first request) | Warm/reused connection |
|---|---|---|
| DNS | Full resolution (or cache miss) | Cached — ~0ms |
| TCP handshake | 1 round-trip | Skipped — reused |
| TLS handshake | 1-2 round-trips | Skipped — reused |
| HTTP request/response | 1 round-trip | 1 round-trip |

**How to decide what to optimize:** if a page feels slow only on first visit, look at DNS/TCP/TLS setup cost; if it's slow on every visit including repeats, the bottleneck is the HTTP exchange or server processing itself, not connection setup.

slides.subTitle: "It's just one extra round-trip"
slides.markdown:
A common mistake is treating DNS/TCP/TLS overhead as negligible compared to "the real work." On a connection with 150ms round-trip latency (common for mobile or cross-continent traffic), a cold HTTPS connection can burn 450-600ms in handshakes alone — before a single byte of the actual page arrives.

This is exactly where real-world web latency hides, and exactly why techniques like connection reuse, TLS session resumption, and CDN edge termination exist — they're not micro-optimizations, they're removing whole round-trips that dominate perceived load time.
